meta.name: The Drip Fund
meta.tagline: Every dividend reinvests. More shares, more dividends, more shares. Slow, steady, relentless compounding. Water wears down stone.
meta.oneJob: A taxable brokerage account with one job: build a growing stream of passive dividend income to supplement retirement. Not the primary retirement vehicle (that's a 401k and Roth IRA) — this is the income supplement: money that shows up every month whether you work or not.
meta.riskTolerance: Moderate — sustainable, growing income over maximum yield
context: Home mortgage is being aggressively paid down — the retirement goal includes zero housing costs.
When the mortgage is paid off, a significant portion of freed cash flow redirects here immediately.
401k and Roth IRA are the primary retirement vehicles; this account is supplemental passive income.

strategyRules.title: DRIP is always on
strategyRules.body: Every dividend reinvests automatically. Never turn it off.

strategyRules.title: New money to the Core Three
strategyRules.body: All new contributions go to JEPI, JEPQ, SCHD only. No impulse buys.

strategyRules.title: Do not chase yield
strategyRules.body: If a yield looks too good to be true (15%+), it probably is.

strategyRules.title: Quality over quantity
strategyRules.body: Fewer, stronger positions beats 20 tiny ones.

strategyRules.title: Redirect mortgage cash flow
strategyRules.body: When the mortgage is paid off, redirect a significant portion of that freed cash flow here immediately.

strategyRules.title: Review quarterly
strategyRules.body: Confirm DRIP is active on all positions. No cash sitting idle in the money market unnecessarily.

strategyRules.title: Don't panic sell on dips
strategyRules.body: If the business is sound, a dip just means cheaper DRIP shares.

strategyRules.title: Tax awareness
strategyRules.body: This is a taxable account. Consider capital-gains implications before selling anything with large unrealized gains (especially AAPL).

strategyRules.title: Check SEC yield vs distribution yield
strategyRules.body: Before ever adding a position. If there's a huge gap, the 'income' is smoke and mirrors. See the QYLG lesson.

yieldTrap.warning: A high distribution yield reflects what was paid, not what will be paid. BDCs and struggling companies often show inflated yields precisely because the market is pricing in risk of cuts or collapse. Always ask: why is the yield this high? If the answer is 'the price has been falling for years,' that is a red flag, not a buying opportunity.
yieldTrap.examples: PSEC and OXSQ both destroyed capital while advertising double-digit yields.
yieldTrap.secLesson: Distribution yield includes option premiums and return of capital. SEC yield measures actual investment income. If a fund shows 19% distribution yield but 0.3% SEC yield, most of what it 'pays' you is your own money handed back in a different pocket — which is why the position loses value over time. Always compare both numbers before deciding.

build.name: Tier 1 — Build
build.subtitle: Monthly contributions go here
build.desc: All new monthly contributions go to these positions only. No new positions without strong justification.

hold.name: Tier 2 — Hold
hold.subtitle: DRIP, do not add
hold.desc: Held and allowed to DRIP. Do not sell, do not add. Let compounding work.

monitor.name: Tier 3 — Monitor
monitor.subtitle: Watch quarterly, may trim
monitor.desc: Watched quarterly. Off-strategy or concentrated positions that may be trimmed.

holdings.name: BP PLC ADR
holdings.why: Yield around 4.2%. Held for income and energy exposure. The share price ran up roughly 19% since June, which pushed BP back up to about 16.4% of the account — not because anything was added, but because it outran everything else. Watch for dividend policy changes.
holdings.risk: Back to being the largest single position at ~16.4%, up from 15.0% in June (still below April's 20.3%). Do not add; the only lever is letting other positions grow. The unrealized gain is now +$1,937, which makes selling even more tax-expensive than it was. BP cut its dividend in 2020.

holdings.name: Schwab US Dividend Equity ETF
holdings.why: Lower yield now but dividend and price grow consistently. The long-game compounder. Most tax-efficient of the Core Three (qualified dividends). Crossed 100 shares this summer and is now up +12.7% — the April mega-buy has fully vindicated itself.

holdings.name: JPMorgan Nasdaq Equity Premium Income ETF
holdings.why: Same covered-call strategy as JEPI but Nasdaq / tech-heavy. Higher yield with more growth upside. Its SEC yield matches its distribution yield — the income is real. Took about half the summer contributions and has moved back ahead of JEPI. Still the single biggest income producer in the account at ~$292/yr.

holdings.name: JPMorgan Equity Premium Income ETF
holdings.why: S&P 500 covered-call ETF. Monthly dividends, quality management, sustainable yield, low volatility. Finally back above cost basis after months underwater — and it collected distributions the whole time it was red. Got no new money this summer, so it is now the smallest of the Core Three and the one to favor next.

holdings.name: Apple Inc
holdings.why: Held for a huge unrealized gain (+$2,199, +531%). Cleared $300/share this summer and is now worth more than six times what it cost. Hold, do not add. Let DRIP work.
holdings.risk: Tax impact of selling is significant given the +531% unrealized gain — consider capital gains before ever trimming.

holdings.name: M&T Bank
holdings.why: Solid regional bank with a growing dividend. Big total gain (+165%) and within a few dollars of a $1,000 unrealized profit on a $603 cost basis.

holdings.name: Neos Nasdaq 100 Hedged ETF
holdings.why: Not a dividend-income play and doesn't fit the strategy cleanly, but the gain has held at about +34% for two straight quarters and it keeps paying monthly.
holdings.risk: Watch. Do not add. Consider selling if the gain erodes below $200 or a better use of capital emerges. It has now survived three quarterly reviews on inertia — decide it or sell it.

holdings.name: Global X S&P 500 Covered Call ETF
holdings.why: The strongest covered-call base (S&P 500) — but redundant next to JEPI, which does the same job with a less punishing structure. Sold on Aug 20, 2026 while the gain was still only $10.68 and the exit was effectively free. Proceeds go to SCHD.
holdings.risk: Sale decided and in flight — settlement pending, so it still appears here as held.

holdings.name: Coca-Cola
holdings.why: 60+ year dividend grower. Never cuts. Boring perfection — and it just crossed $1,000 on nothing but price growth and reinvested dividends.

holdings.name: Wells Fargo
holdings.why: Recovered well, dividend growing again. Massive total gain (+211%) on a $310 cost basis. Share count is flat since June simply because the next quarterly dividend doesn't land until September.

holdings.name: Realty Income Corp
holdings.why: 'The Monthly Dividend Company.' 30+ years of dividend increases. Monthly payer. Real estate diversification. Now the only red position in the account — which is exactly when a monthly DRIP earns its keep, buying cheaper shares twelve times a year.

holdings.name: Schwab International Dividend Equity ETF
holdings.why: International diversification — the global cousin of SCHD. Adds non-US exposure to an otherwise all-domestic portfolio. Finally back to break-even after five months of going essentially nowhere.

holdings.name: Annaly Capital Management
holdings.why: Mortgage REIT, acceptable risk at the current small size, yields well. Nearly a full extra share added by DRIP since June, with no dividend cut so far.
holdings.risk: Mortgage REITs are interest-rate sensitive and have historically cut dividends. The high distribution yield warrants skepticism. Position is small (~$677). Watch Fed policy quarterly.

pending.title: Selling XYLD, proceeds to SCHD
pending.status: Decided and in flight. The sale has to settle before the cash can buy SCHD, so for a couple of days this page still shows XYLD as a held position — the numbers below are accurate as of the last snapshot, not as of the decision.

why.b: JEPI already covers S&P 500 covered calls. Two funds were being paid to do one job, and XYLD was the weaker of the two.

why.t: It has the worst structure in the category
why.b: XYLD writes at-the-money calls on essentially the entire portfolio, which caps upside harder than any alternative. JEPI writes further out through ELNs and keeps more of a rally.

why.t: It was the QYLG lesson, again
why.b: Same Global X mechanism, same bargain: a headline yield funded by giving away the upside. That lesson already cost money once. Holding XYLD was paying tuition twice.

why.t: The exit was free, and wouldn't stay that way
why.b: The position was up $10.68 — roughly $1.60 of tax. Every month held, the gain grows and the exit gets more expensive. Cheap exits have a shelf life.
Eleven years from retirement with every dividend reinvested, capped upside is the wrong trade. Current income matters at 65, not at 54.

why.t: SCHD is the better home for the money
why.b: It cuts covered-call concentration from ~28% to ~24%, and SCHD pays qualified dividends where XYLD did not — a meaningful difference in a taxable account.

pending.tradeoff: This deliberately lowers estimated income by about $79/yr — XYLD paid roughly $116, the same money in SCHD pays about $37. That is the point rather than a side effect: trading current yield for total return and a lower tax bill. It does narrow the dividends-vs-contributions crossover back to a hair above the ~$1,200/yr that gets contributed by hand.
pending.rule: Consistent with the standing rules: quality over quantity, don't chase yield, and check SEC yield against distribution yield before holding anything.

coreThree.note: All new monthly contributions split between these three — together about 39% of the account. SCHD is the clear leader; the summer's contributions went to SCHD and JEPQ, which leaves JEPI as the underweighted one to favor next.

contribution.split: Roughly equal thirds into JEPI, JEPQ, SCHD; any extra to whichever is most underweighted.
contribution.tip: Fidelity allows dollar-based fractional purchases — type '$67' instead of a share count.

concentrationNotes.title: BP concentration (moved the wrong way)
concentrationNotes.body: BP is back to about 16.4% of the portfolio, up from ~15.0% in June, though still below April's ~20.3% peak. Nothing was added — the price simply rose roughly 19% and outgrew the rest of the account. The plan doesn't change: do not add, keep growing everything else, and let time dilute it. The +$1,937 unrealized gain makes selling tax-expensive. BP cut its dividend in 2020.

concentrationNotes.title: Covered-call concentration
concentrationNotes.body: The portfolio holds JEPI, JEPQ, and XYLD — three covered-call products (together about 28% of the account). In a strong bull market, covered calls cap upside. An accepted tradeoff for consistent monthly income.

concentrationNotes.title: NLY interest-rate risk
concentrationNotes.body: Mortgage REITs are rate-sensitive and have historically cut dividends. NLY's distribution yield is high enough to warrant skepticism. Position is small (~$677). Watch Fed policy quarterly.

projections.assumptions: Assumes 9% total annual return, 6% blended yield, starting value ~$24,200.
projections.caveat: These projections are optimistic. A covered-call-heavy portfolio may deliver yield but underperform on growth in strong bull markets. A more conservative, realistic target is roughly $450–550/month of income by year 10 at $300/month contributions.
